patient.history_present_illness: Mr. B. is a 61-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C), prior HCC treated with TACE, and a prior HE episode 4 months ago now on rifaximin prophylaxis, brought by his daughter for acute confusion and agitation over the preceding 24 hours. His daughter reported he was found disoriented in the bathroom at 2 AM, had been slurring his speech since yesterday evening, and had been combative and uncooperative throughout the morning. She found an empty vodka bottle in his room, and he admitted on direct questioning to having drunk 'a little yesterday.' His serum ethanol level on arrival was 14 mg/dL — a low but detectable level. He had last been seen by hepatology 3 weeks ago when labs showed stable MELD 18. Over the prior week, his daughter noticed decreasing oral intake, reduced rifaximin adherence (ran out 5 days ago and had not refilled), and increasing abdominal distension. He denied hematemesis or melena. Temperature 37.9°C raised concern for possible infection as a precipitant. The combination of low-level ethanol exposure, rifaximin non-adherence for 5 days, fever, and tachycardia created a moderate-difficulty clinical scenario with multiple potential precipitants requiring careful evaluation. Precipitant was ultimately determined to be combined: alcohol use (direct neurotoxin + ammoniagenic substrate) and rifaximin non-adherence with possible SBP.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, grade 3, alcoholic cirrhosis — precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (PMN 310/mm3) + acute alcohol use + rifaximin non-adherence

differential.key_features: Serum ethanol 14 mg/dL — recent alcohol use; contributes to confusion; but HE is primary given ammonia 88 + SBP; alcohol withdrawal risk also present
SBP confirmed (PMN 310) — septic encephalopathy and HE coexist; SBP is the precipitant
Thiamine 42 (deficient) in active alcoholic; but MRI no periaqueductal changes; treat empirically with IV thiamine
CT head no hemorrhage; no trauma history

optimal_actions.action: IV thiamine 500 mg BEFORE any dextrose — active alcoholic with thiamine 42
CT head — exclude hemorrhage (thrombocytopenia + coagulopathy risk)
Labs — ammonia, LFTs, CBC, coags, toxicology, ethanol

optimal_actions.expected_finding: PMN 310 — SBP CONFIRMED; start ceftriaxone + albumin immediately

optimal_actions.action: Restart rifaximin 550 mg BID + lactulose 30 mL TID

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Generalized slowing — HE/metabolic encephalopathy pattern; no NCSE

critical_actions: Paracentesis is mandatory in any cirrhotic with ascites + confusion + fever — SBP (PMN 310) is the primary precipitant and requires immediate antibiotics + albumin
Albumin administration with SBP treatment: 1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3 — prevents hepatorenal syndrome in SBP
IV thiamine before ANY dextrose-containing fluid — alcoholic with thiamine 42 nmol/L (deficient); Wernicke risk real
Avoid benzodiazepines as sedatives — worsen HE; concurrent alcohol withdrawal risk requires careful lowest-effective-dose lorazepam with CIWA monitoring
contraindicated_actions: Diazepam or chlordiazepoxide for alcohol withdrawal — accumulate in cirrhosis; use lorazepam or phenobarbital
Benzodiazepines as anxiolytics without CIWA indication — will precipitate/worsen HE
Dextrose before thiamine in alcoholic patient
key_reasoning_points: SBP can present with grade 3 HE without classic peritoneal signs — abdominal exam may be unremarkable; paracentesis must not be delayed by clinical suspicion threshold
Multiple concurrent precipitants of HE are common: this case has alcohol (direct neurotoxin), SBP (cytokines + ammonia), and rifaximin non-adherence — each contributes independently
Concurrent alcohol withdrawal and HE is a challenging dual diagnosis — alcohol withdrawal worsening tracked separately by CIWA; benzodiazepine use in liver failure requires careful monitoring
Albumin infusion with SBP treatment is a critical intervention that reduces hepatorenal syndrome risk by 50% — evidence-based standard of care
